chapters.title: Chapter 3: Completing and Stress-Testing the DCF

lessons.title: From Enterprise Value to Value per Share

children.text: In the last lesson, Kaveri Ridge Cement's DCF produced an enterprise value of ₹8,054 crore. It is tempting to subtract net debt, divide by the share count and call it done. That shortcut is where many careful DCFs lose their accuracy. Between enterprise value and the number you compare with the NSE price sits a bridge of items that live in the notes to the accounts: investments, leases, minority shareholders, employee obligations, disputed tax demands and stock options. This lesson walks across that bridge, one item at a time.

body.text: Enterprise value is the value of the operating business only. To reach value per share, add everything shareholders own that the cash flows left out, subtract every claim that ranks ahead of them or alongside them, and divide by every share that will exist.

children.text: The Bridge

body.latex: \text{Equity value} = \text{EV} + \text{Non-operating assets} - \text{Debt and debt-like claims} - \text{Non-controlling interest}
body.caption: Then: value per share = (equity value + option exercise proceeds) ÷ diluted shares

children.text: The rule behind every item is consistency with your cash flows. If something generated cash that is already inside FCFF, it is already inside enterprise value. Adding it again double counts. If something will cost shareholders money but was left out of FCFF, it must come out now.
What You Add

body.caption: Non-operating assets: value not captured in FCFF

cells: Cash and liquid investments
Interest on surplus cash is not part of operating profit, so its value sits outside EV
Margin money deposits and escrow balances that are not freely available; cash needed to run daily operations
Stakes in associates and joint ventures
Only the share of profit, not the cash flows, of these companies is reported; they are not in FCFF
Use market value for listed stakes; consider a holding discount and tax on any sale
Surplus land and non-core property
Not used in operations, so it generates no FCFF
Use a realistic value net of tax and selling costs, not historical cost
Other non-operating investments
Mutual fund units, bonds or strategic stakes held outside the core business
Check the investments note for what is actually held and at what value

children.text: What You Subtract

body.caption: Claims that rank ahead of or alongside equity shareholders

cells: Borrowings
Lenders are paid before shareholders. Include current maturities of long-term debt.
Borrowings notes, both non-current and current
Lease liabilities
Under Ind AS 116, lease payments sit in financing, outside FCFF, so the liability is debt-like
Lease liabilities line on the balance sheet and the leases note
Non-controlling interest
Consolidated cash flows include 100% of subsidiaries, but outside shareholders own part of them
Consolidated balance sheet, equity section
Preference shares
Rank ahead of equity shareholders for dividends and repayment
Share capital or borrowings notes
Unfunded employee benefit obligations
Gratuity and leave encashment owed to employees but not yet funded
Employee benefits note under Ind AS 19
Contingent liabilities
Disputed tax, regulatory and legal demands that may have to be paid
Contingent liabilities and commitments note
Guarantees for group companies
Can become real debt if the group company defaults
Contingent liabilities note and related party note

body.text: Do not subtract trade payables, provisions for normal operating expenses or other working capital items. They are already reflected in FCFF through the change in working capital. Subtracting them again double counts.

Use consolidated financial statements for both the DCF and the bridge. Most Indian listed companies report standalone and consolidated numbers. If you forecast consolidated cash flows but subtract standalone debt, or the reverse, the bridge will not match the business you valued.

children.text: The Line Item Most Investors Skip: Contingent Liabilities
A
contingent liability

is a claim the company disputes and has not recorded as a liability. In India, disputed income tax, GST, customs, royalty and regulatory demands can be very large relative to a company's size, and they can take a decade or more to resolve through appellate tribunals and courts.

markDefs.definition: A possible obligation that depends on an uncertain future event, such as the outcome of a tax dispute or lawsuit. It is disclosed in the notes rather than recorded on the balance sheet, unless payment becomes probable.

children.text: The Indian telecom industry learned how real these numbers can become. For years, operators disputed the Department of Telecommunications' broad definition of adjusted gross revenue (AGR), on which licence fees and spectrum charges are calculated. When the Supreme Court upheld the government's definition, disputed amounts turned into enormous payable dues overnight.

body.title: The AGR dispute: from note to the accounts to balance sheet crisis

events.title: The dispute begins
events.description: Operators challenge the government's inclusion of non-telecom income in adjusted gross revenue. The amounts are disclosed and contested for years.

events.title: Supreme Court ruling
events.description: The Supreme Court upholds the Department of Telecommunications' definition of AGR. Industry dues, including interest and penalties, run into more than ₹1 lakh crore.

events.title: Payment schedule
events.description: The Supreme Court allows operators ten years to pay the dues, with an initial instalment payable upfront.

events.title: Lasting damage
events.description: Vodafone Idea, carrying one of the largest AGR burdens, repeatedly sought relief. The government later converted part of its dues into an equity stake in the company.

children.text: The lesson for valuation: never ignore the contingent liabilities note. For each large item, estimate the probability of paying and the likely amount, and subtract the expected value. Where a single dispute could threaten the company, value it in scenarios rather than as one probability-weighted number.
Worked Example: Kaveri Ridge Cement's Bridge

The notes to Kaveri Ridge's consolidated accounts reveal several items. It owns 26% of a listed ready-mix concrete company, currently worth ₹240 crore at market price. It holds surplus land near Mysuru worth an estimated ₹120 crore after tax on sale. It has lease liabilities on a warehouse and rail sidings, a 51% subsidiary that runs a grinding unit, an unfunded gratuity obligation and a ₹900 crore disputed mining royalty and GST demand, which its lawyers consider roughly a 50:50 case.

body.caption: Kaveri Ridge Cement: enterprise value to equity value (₹ crore, illustrative)

cells: Enterprise value (DCF)
Add: cash and liquid investments
Add: 26% stake in listed associate, at market value
Add: surplus land, net of estimated tax
Less: borrowings, including current maturities
Less: lease liabilities
Less: non-controlling interest in grinding subsidiary
Less: unfunded gratuity obligation
Less: expected contingent liability (₹900 × 50%)
Equity value

body.text: Non-controlling interest is shown at book value here for simplicity. Where a subsidiary is large or much more valuable than its book value, estimate the minority shareholders' share of the subsidiary's market or intrinsic value instead.

children.text: Dividing by the Right Number of Shares
Kaveri Ridge has

25 crore shares outstanding, but it has also granted employees 0.60 crore stock options at an exercise price of ₹150. If the shares are worth more than ₹150, those options will be exercised and existing shareholders will own a smaller slice. A simple and consistent way to handle this is the
if-exercised method
: add the cash employees would pay to exercise, and add the new shares.

markDefs.definition: A way to account for in-the-money stock options: assume they are exercised, add the exercise proceeds to equity value and add the new shares to the share count.

stats.label: If the royalty dispute is lost in full

children.text: The full bridge cuts value per share by about 5% compared with the shortcut, mostly because of the royalty dispute. Against a market price of ₹300, the stock already looked expensive on the DCF. The bridge makes that conclusion stronger, and the worst-case figure shows how much of the gap depends on a single legal outcome.

body.caption: Share count adjustments to check in the annual report

cells: Stock options and RSUs (ESOP note under Ind AS 102)
Add in-the-money options using the if-exercised or treasury stock method
Compulsorily convertible instruments (CCDs, CCPS, warrants)
Add shares that will be issued on conversion, and any conversion proceeds
FCCBs and other optionally convertible bonds
Treat as debt if conversion is unlikely, as shares if conversion price is well below value
Shares held by an ESOP trust
Usually already excluded from shares outstanding in the accounts; avoid counting them twice
Partly paid shares
Include, and add any uncalled amount as proceeds

body.text: New-age technology listings in India often have large ESOP pools, sometimes several percent of total shares. Using the basic share count for such companies can overstate value per share materially.

children.text: Check Your Understanding

body.title: Build a simple bridge
body.prompt: A hospital chain has an enterprise value of ₹5,000 crore, cash of ₹400 crore, borrowings of ₹1,200 crore, lease liabilities of ₹100 crore and non-controlling interest of ₹150 crore. It has 10 crore shares and no options. What is its value per share, in ₹?
body.explanation: Equity value = ₹5,000 + ₹400 - ₹1,200 - ₹100 - ₹150 = ₹3,950 crore. Value per share = ₹3,950 crore ÷ 10 crore shares = ₹395.

body.title: Adjust for stock options
body.prompt: A software company's equity value is ₹2,000 crore. It has 10 crore basic shares and 0.5 crore in-the-money employee stock options with an exercise price of ₹100. Using the if-exercised method, what is its diluted value per share, in ₹? Answer to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Proceeds = 0.5 crore × ₹100 = ₹50 crore. Diluted value per share = (₹2,000 + ₹50) ÷ (10 + 0.5) = ₹195.24, compared with ₹200.00 on basic shares.

body.title: What does not belong in the bridge?
body.question: You have valued a consumer durables company using FCFF, with working capital changes included. Which item should you NOT subtract from enterprise value?
body.explanation: Trade payables are part of working capital, which is already reflected in FCFF through the change in net working capital. Subtracting them again would double count. Borrowings, lease liabilities and unfunded employee obligations are claims outside FCFF.

body.title: Outside shareholders in subsidiaries
body.textWithBlank: When a DCF uses consolidated cash flows, the share of subsidiaries owned by outside shareholders, called ___ interest, must be subtracted.
body.explanation: Consolidated accounts include 100% of each subsidiary's cash flows, even where the parent owns less than 100%. The portion owned by others is non-controlling interest, often still called minority interest.

body.title: The cash-rich infrastructure company
body.scenario: Deepa, a Bengaluru-based investor, is valuing a listed infrastructure developer. Its balance sheet shows ₹3,000 crore of cash, which makes the stock look cheap on an EV basis. Reading the notes, she finds: ₹1,800 crore of the cash is margin money and escrow deposits held against bank guarantees and project obligations; the contingent liabilities note lists ₹5,000 crore of disputed tax and arbitration claims, described by management as "not probable"; the company has given ₹4,000 crore of corporate guarantees for loans taken by two promoter group companies, one of which has recently had its rating downgraded; and the consolidated balance sheet shows non-controlling interest of ₹600 crore.
body.prompt: How should Deepa treat each of these items in her bridge from enterprise value to equity value?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Cash: add only freely available cash. The ₹1,800 crore of margin money and escrow deposits is tied to obligations and cannot be distributed to shareholders, so she should add about ₹1,200 crore, not ₹3,000 crore.
2. Contingent liabilities: "not probable" is management's view, not a zero. She should read each major item, estimate probabilities and likely settlement amounts, and subtract the expected value. For any single claim that could be large relative to equity, she should also run a downside scenario.
3. Corporate guarantees: these are the most dangerous item. A guarantee for a group company that has just been downgraded could become real debt. She should estimate the probability that the guarantees are called, subtract an expected amount, and treat this as a governance red flag in her cost of equity or scenarios.
4. Non-controlling interest: subtract the ₹600 crore, or better, estimate the outside shareholders' share of the subsidiaries' value if they are worth much more than book.

The overall conclusion: the "cash-rich" label is misleading. After restricting cash and allowing for contingent claims and guarantees, the equity value could be far lower than the headline EV calculation suggests.

body.title: Build the bridge from an annual report
steps: Confirm your DCF used consolidated figures, and use the consolidated balance sheet for every bridge item.
From the borrowings notes, add non-current borrowings and current borrowings, including current maturities of long-term debt.
From the leases note, find lease liabilities and confirm lease payments were excluded from your FCFF.
From the investments and cash notes, separate freely available cash and non-operating investments from restricted balances.
From the consolidated balance sheet, find non-controlling interest.
From the employee benefits note, find any unfunded gratuity or pension obligation.
Read the contingent liabilities and commitments note in full, including guarantees, and estimate an expected amount for material items.
From the share capital and ESOP notes, build a diluted share count.

cards.definition: The value of the operating business to all capital providers, from discounting FCFF at WACC.
Assets whose value is not in FCFF, such as surplus cash, associate stakes and surplus land. Added to EV.
Debt-like obligations under Ind AS 116. Subtracted when lease payments are outside FCFF.
The share of consolidated subsidiaries owned by outside shareholders. Subtracted from EV.
A disputed or possible obligation disclosed in the notes. Subtract its expected value.
Add in-the-money option proceeds to equity value and the new shares to the share count.

points: Enterprise value covers only the operating business. The bridge to equity value lives in the notes to the accounts.
Add non-operating assets not captured in FCFF: freely available cash, associate stakes, surplus land and other investments.
Subtract borrowings, lease liabilities, non-controlling interest, preference shares, unfunded employee obligations and the expected cost of contingent liabilities and guarantees.
Never subtract working capital items such as trade payables. They are already in FCFF.
Use consolidated figures consistently, and read the contingent liabilities note in full. India's AGR dispute shows how quickly disputed amounts can become real.
Divide by a diluted share count that includes in-the-money options and convertible instruments.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Kaveri Ridge Cement Ltd, the other companies described and the individuals named are fictional, and their figures are illustrative. The AGR dispute summary is simplified and approximate, and references to real companies are historical, not recommendations. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making investment decisions.
